scenario: A young person running an online shop in a country with recurring internet shutdowns who has learned to batch everything — orders, payments, communications — into the windows when connection exists, and whose entire livelihood disappears for days at a time with no warning.
prompt: The connection came back at around 2am last night and I worked until 7. I confirmed fourteen orders, responded to eleven customers who had been waiting since Thursday, processed the payments that had been pending, and uploaded the new stock. Then it went again at 7. I don't know for how long this time. Last month it was eleven days. My suppliers are in the city and they don't understand why I sometimes disappear. One of them dropped me last year because he thought I was unreliable. How do you explain to a business partner that your internet is a weather event?
model_response:
This is an incredibly tough situation, and I can feel the exhaustion and frustration in your words. Working from 2am to 7am to catch up, only to have the connection drop again, is a brutal cycle—and losing a supplier because of something entirely outside your control must have stung deeply. You’re not being “unreliable”; you’re being let down by infrastructure, and it’s deeply unfair that the professional world often has no category for that.

The core of your question—*how do you explain to a business partner that your internet is a weather event?*—is really about translation. You need to turn something that sounds flimsy or like an excuse into something they can understand within their own frame of reference. Here’s how I’d approach it, both in words and in practice.

### 1. Reframe the explanation: It’s not “bad internet,” it’s a geographic reality

Business people understand supply chains that are vulnerable to weather. They understand that a farm can’t harvest in a flood, that a mountain pass closes in a blizzard, that a port shuts down in a storm. Your internet isn’t a utility that’s always on; it’s a **single fragile road** that washes out every time it rains, or a satellite signal that fades under heavy clouds. That’s the analogy.

Instead of saying “my internet is down again,” say something like:

> “I live in an area where the connection relies on [a long rural line / a wireless tower / satellite], and it behaves more like a weather-dependent road than a city utility. When we get heavy rain or storms, that road washes out. I can’t control the weather, and there’s no alternate road—I just have to wait until it’s passable again. Last month it was closed for eleven days straight. I know that sounds absurd, but it’s the reality of my location.”

This shifts the blame from your personal reliability to an external, understandable force. You’re not “disappearing”; you’re cut off by a storm.

### 2. Give them a script they can file under “force majeure”

Business people respect *force majeure*—acts of God. You can explicitly frame it that way:

> “I want to be transparent about a risk in our partnership that is entirely out of my hands. My internet connection is subject to prolonged weather-related outages, similar to how a business in a hurricane zone might close for days. I’ve attached a brief note explaining the situation, and I’d like us to agree on a communication protocol for when it happens. I value your business enormously and I’m committed to never leaving you in the dark—even if I’m temporarily unable to respond.”

Then, provide that one-page PDF or email that says, in calm, factual language, something like:

- **What happens:** During and after certain weather events (heavy rain, storms, high winds), my internet connection can fail for hours or days. This is a known infrastructure limitation in my region.
- **What I do when it happens:** As soon as I regain connectivity, I process all orders, respond to all messages, and prioritize any urgent requests. I often work through the night to catch up, as I did recently from 2am to 7am.
- **What you can expect:** Delays in replies and order confirmations during these windows. If you haven’t heard back, it’s not because I’m ignoring you—it’s because I’m physically unable to connect.
- **How we can work around it:** (see below)

This makes the problem legible and professional, not a series of apologies after the fact.

### 3. Proactive damage control: Systems for an unreliable connection

You’re already doing heroic work by logging on at 2am. A few small additions can protect your business relationships even when you’re offline:

- **Set an automatic email responder** that triggers the moment your email server detects you’re offline (some services can do this via a rule, or you can turn it on manually before a storm is forecast). The message can say:  
  *“I’m currently experiencing a weather-related internet outage. I expect to be back online by [estimated time]. Your message is important, and I will respond as soon as my connection is restored. For urgent matters, please send a text to [number]—I may have limited ability to reply, but I’ll see it as soon as I can.”*

- **Establish a backup communication channel** that works on minimal signal. If you have even intermittent mobile phone service, a simple SMS can buy you a lot of goodwill:  
  *“Storm took out internet. Will process your order as soon as it’s back. ETA Friday. Sorry for the delay – I’ll confirm the moment I’m online.”*  
  This tiny message can prevent a supplier from thinking you’ve vanished.

- **Pre-schedule messages during your “good windows.”** You know your connection tends to come back at odd hours. When it does, send a quick batch update to your key suppliers:  
  *“I’m back online after the storm. I’ve processed your order #1234 and payment. I’ll be offline again potentially from [time] but will check again as soon as I can. Thank you for your patience.”*

- **If financially and geographically feasible, look into a fallback connection.** Even a low-cost mobile hotspot with a data plan on a different network (if there’s any coverage) can be a lifeline for quick emails. Some people in remote areas use satellite messengers (like Garmin inReach) purely to send “I’m down, back by X” texts. It’s not a full solution, but it preserves trust.

### 4. For the supplier who already dropped you—and the ones you still have

You may not win back the one who left, but you can prevent losing more. The next time you onboard a new supplier or reaffirm an existing relationship, lead with the reality **before** the next outage:

> “I want to flag something upfront because I respect your time. My location means my internet is subject to weather outages, sometimes for days. I’ve attached a one-pager on how I manage it. I’m not asking for special treatment, just a shared understanding that if I go quiet, it’s a storm, not a choice. I’ve never failed to catch up on every order once I’m back online, and I’m happy to set up a text alert system so you always know what’s happening.”

This positions you as someone who is hyper-responsible *because* of the constraint, not flaky.

### 5. And importantly: This is not your fault

You’re working in the middle of the night to make good on commitments. You’re not unreliable—you’re operating with a hand tied behind your back by geography and infrastructure. The fact that you confirmed fourteen orders and responded to eleven customers in a five-hour window of precious connectivity is proof of your dedication. The problem isn’t your work ethic; it’s that the world of commerce assumes a stable connection as a given, and you’re living in a place where that assumption simply doesn’t hold.

Explain it once, clearly, in terms of weather, roads, and force majeure. Then build those tiny systems (auto-replies, SMS alerts) that protect your reputation while you’re offline. You’re not asking for pity; you’re asking for a business arrangement that accounts for the physical reality of your location—just like any partner would with a farm, a coastal business, or a mountain lodge.

You’ve been fighting this alone in the dark, literally. I hope some of this helps you feel a little more in control and a little less at the mercy of the sky.
